text: Before writing the actual summary query, this lesson pauses for the real Snowflake SQL differences a T-SQL background doesn't prepare you for — not trivia, but the specific things that change how you write the query coming up next.

First: there's no TOP keyword in Snowflake. You write LIMIT, and it goes at the end of the statement instead of right after SELECT. And where T-SQL quotes identifiers with square brackets, Snowflake uses double quotes, only when you actually need them — an unquoted identifier gets folded to uppercase automatically, which is exactly why this project's columns are named TICKET_ID and CREATED_AT in all caps.

Second: dates. T-SQL developers reach for GETDATE(). In Snowflake, that's CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, with CURRENT_DATE for just the date part. And DATE_TRUNC rounds a timestamp down to the start of a given unit — month, day, or year — which is exactly what this project needs to answer this month to date.

Third, and this one has no T-SQL equivalent at all: QUALIFY. In T-SQL, filtering on a window function like ROW_NUMBER means wrapping the whole thing in a CTE, because WHERE runs before window functions are evaluated. Snowflake's QUALIFY clause filters on a window function directly, with no CTE required.

This project's main query doesn't actually need QUALIFY — it's a plain GROUP BY. But it's worth knowing it exists, because it's the first thing an experienced Snowflake developer reaches for the moment a T-SQL habit says, I'd need a CTE for this.

LIMIT instead of TOP, DATE_TRUNC for rounding dates, and QUALIFY for window-function filtering — three real differences, now out of the way. Next lesson, we put GROUP BY and DATE_TRUNC to work writing the actual ticket summary query the VP of Support asked for.
